newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Aznar sees $1 bln credit line for Argentine soon.
newsitem.headline: Aznar sees $1 bln credit line for Argentine soon.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar promised that Spain's parliament would soon give its approval to a new economic cooperation pact with Argentina that will include a $1 billion soft credit line.
Aznar said in Buenos Aires, on the last day of a three-day visit to help along flourishing bilateral trade, that the cooperation agreement was approved by his cabinet on April 11.

"A credit for Argentina with favorable conditions for $1 billion is part of that cooperation agreement that is already in the process of being ratified by the Spanish parliament," the Spanish leader told a packed news conference.
Aznar was accompanied by 60 Spanish businessmen, including 40 from smaller firms, on his first trip as prime minister.

He was full of praise for the economy of Argentina, the top destination of Spanish exports, buying 15 percent of them. Spanish firms have spent $1.4 billion on privatizations here and 12 top Spanish firms invested $7.0 billion from 1991-96.
That is expected to grow to $11.5 billion by end-1999.

"Spanish investment trusts in Argentina," said Aznar. "Obviously Spain is very interested and will continue participating in the privatization process in Argentina, which is having obvious success and attracting fierce competition."
Spanish firms already have a major stake in Argentina's telecommunications, air transport, energy and power sectors, as well as banking, fishing and the food industry.

But Aznar listed upcoming privatizations of Argentina's post office and airports as key areas of interest, and went on to register Spanish interest in construction and engineering and "all areas where it is possible."
He also pledged that Spain would lobby the European Union to help strengthen the regional trade bloc Mercosur, formed by Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Brazil, which he visited before Argentina.

Aznar described Mercosur's economic and political success as "spectacular" but also dwelt on a recent trade spat between Brazil and its Mercosur partners, in which Brazil was reluctant to exclude them from new limits in import financing.

"It affected a range of Argentine products and had an impact on the meaning for the future of Mercosur. It also affected Spain," he said. "I cannot understand protectionist measures. There may be moments when they are necessary for a particular reason, but I am in favor of free trade."
